summary:
The Komi Republic stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which extends in full. The sources record no republic-level variation in how these laws operate, and the jurisdiction is assessed at the national score. A trans visitor to Syktyvkar or anywhere else in the Komi Republic faces the same legal position as a trans visitor elsewhere in the country.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and foreign government warnings issued to LGBT travellers say so.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. An independent media outlet reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, on 17 January 2024, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. A foreign broadcaster's report of 27 July 2024 followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The US State Department travel advisory advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. That finding rests on country-wide evidence; the sources identify no Chechnya-specific regime applying to the Komi Republic.

Raids, extremism charges and arrests defined LGBTQ+ life in the country through 2025, according to a national newspaper report of 23 June 2025, in which a St Petersburg queer woman described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing the country.

The general travel advisories in force describe risks that extend beyond LGBT-specific law, including wrongful detention of foreign nationals, arbitrary law enforcement and the war. These are adjacent to the trans-specific assessment rather than evidence about it, and they apply to travellers regardless of personal characteristic.

Human Rights Watch reported at least 101 extremism-related convictions nationally against a backdrop in which a designated organisation's alleged symbols are treated as evidence of participation, meaning that a badge, print or image can itself ground a charge.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Komi Republic are affected by the same instrument set as visitors, but with consequences that do not end at the border. Legal gender recognition is unavailable: gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Human Rights Watch's count of at least 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, and the UK Home Office's record of at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, describe the resident population rather than travellers. Roughly 98 of those convictions were administrative, including 81 people convicted under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, while article 282.2 charges carry up to 12 years.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, and that the state is able but unwilling to protect them. The sources identify no republic-level protection machinery, complaint route or hate-crime provision operating in the Komi Republic specifically.

Conversion practice is documented against transgender residents in the country: a case reported on 27 July 2024 describes nine months of confinement, forced testosterone administration and forced labour at a centre near Novosibirsk. Whether any such facility operates in the Komi Republic is not sourced here.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records enforcement of the propaganda, extremism or document provisions within the Komi Republic itself. Whether charges have been brought in Syktyvkar or any other district of the republic is unresolved and not sourced.

Republic-level detail on police practice, access to legal representation, and the availability of shelter or medical care for trans visitors is not sourced. The absence of such material should not be read as evidence that these services exist or do not exist.

The relationship between the 2023 federal prohibitions and any republic-level administrative acts of the Komi Republic is not addressed by the sources, and no sub-national deviation has been identified either way.

The status of hate-crime sentencing enhancement for offences motivated by gender identity, and any republic-level non-discrimination instrument, remains unresolved and not sourced here.
